confidence_note: The three dimensions are the book's core and well attested. The 37% figure and the doubled retention come from Seligman & Schulman's 1986 paper, which the book reports. Creedon's approach and the 'special force' (129 people; 21% and 57%) rest on a Fortune excerpt and trade press, not the book text I could read, so medium. Old text's sample sentences are not quoted as the book's. The 88% decile figure is omitted.
facts: Seligman describes explanatory style along three dimensions: permanence (always vs. this time), pervasiveness (everything vs. this one area), personalization (my fault vs. the circumstances).
Pessimists explain bad events as permanent, pervasive and their own fault; optimists as temporary, specific and not wholly their fault.
For good events the pattern reverses: optimists see a success as lasting and their own doing; pessimists put it down to luck or the circumstances of the day.
Met Life's president, John Creedon, came to Seligman because the company lost many new agents; selling insurance means facing refusal after refusal.
Seligman's questionnaire measured how agents explained bad events. Agents in the top half sold 37% more insurance in their first two years than those in the bottom half.
Seligman and his colleague Peter Schulman published the Met Life results in 1986 in a psychology journal.
In a later group of new hires, top-half scorers stayed in the job at twice the rate of the bottom half.

Met Life also hired a 'special force' of 129 applicants who had failed the industry's career-profile test but scored as strong optimists; they outsold the pessimists in the regular force by 21% in the first year and 57% in the second.
scene_details: an agent hearing 'no' on the phone, call after call
a questionnaire about imagined bad events
129 people hired despite failing the standard test
tension: Met Life hired people its own test had rejected, because of how they explained a 'no'.
opening_idea: Open with the 129 applicants who failed the industry test and were hired anyway, on the strength of a questionnaire about explanations.

lessons.idea: Check the three words in your explanation of a setback: always, everything, me; replace each with what is actually true.
lessons.anchor: agents who explained refusals as temporary and specific sold more and stayed longer

reflect_final: Think of your last real setback: which word in your own explanation of it, always, everything or me, would you now change?

use_cases.situation: A colleague says after a lost client 'I'm just bad at sales'
use_cases.move: Ask what was specific to this case and what will be different with the next one.

use_cases.situation: Team debrief after a failed launch
use_cases.move: Mention that Met Life's optimistic agents sold more because they explained a 'no' as about this call; separate this time from always.

use_cases.situation: You fail an exam or interview
use_cases.move: Write the explanation and circle any always/everything/me; rewrite it.

pocket_idea: Seligman's salespeople heard the same no; the ones who said 'this time' kept dialing.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Met Life hired 129 people who had failed its test, because they explained rejection well, and they outsold the pessimists.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Met Life losing agents; Seligman's questionnaire; top half sold 37% more; special force 21%/57%; three dimensions.
